items.q: A student has three free hours on Saturday and wants to study, work a paid shift and see friends. What does this show?
options: Economic growth, because she finds more uses for her time
Scarcity: limited time forces a choice among wants
An economic system answering the question of for whom to produce
A command decision by the student's parents
A factor of production called entrepreneurship

why.correct: Time is limited and the wants are not, so the student must choose.
options: Growth would mean more time or resources; she still has three hours, so choosing among her wants is scarcity.
Right: a limited resource and competing wants.
Economic systems answer questions for a whole society.
Nothing says anyone else decides.
The student is not organizing a business or taking a business risk.

items.q: An economy spends more of its resources this year on factories and machines and less on consumer goods. What happens to its PPC in the future?
options: It shifts in, because people have fewer consumer goods today
It stays where it is, because total resources are unchanged
It shifts out for consumer goods and in for capital goods
It shifts out farther, because the extra capital raises future production
It becomes a straight line

why.correct: Capital goods made today add to the resources of tomorrow, so the future PPC shifts out more than it would have.
options: Choosing capital goods over consumer goods is a movement along today's curve, not a loss of resources.
The new capital adds to future resources.
More capital raises what the economy can make of both goods, so the curve shifts outward; no part of it moves in.
Right: more capital today means more production possible later.
The shape depends on how suited resources are to each good, not on this choice.

items.q: Two countries have the same opportunity cost of wheat in terms of cloth. What does this imply about trade between them?
options: The country with the absolute advantage gains, and the other loses
Neither gains from specializing and trading these goods
Both gain a great deal
The larger country gains and the smaller loses
They gain as long as the terms of trade are set high enough

why.correct: Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity costs. With equal costs, there is no price at which both do better than making the goods themselves.
options: Gains from trade come from different opportunity costs; with equal costs neither country gains, whoever has the absolute advantage.
Right: no difference in costs, no gain.
Gains need different opportunity costs.
Size does not create comparative advantage.
With equal costs there is no range between them for the terms of trade.

items.q: Why does the demand curve slope downward?
options: Sellers offer less at lower prices, so buyers buy less
Buyers' incomes rise whenever a price falls
Each extra unit costs sellers more to make
A lower price lets buyers afford more (income effect) and makes the good cheaper than its alternatives (substitution effect)
A lower price attracts new sellers into the market

why.correct: Two effects explain the law of demand: a lower price raises buyers' purchasing power (income effect) and makes the good a better deal than substitutes (substitution effect).
options: Demand describes buyers; sellers' behavior is a separate curve.
A lower price raises what incomes can buy, but the incomes themselves do not change.
Rising cost per unit explains why supply slopes up; the demand curve is about buyers' choices at each price.
Right: the income and substitution effects.
Sellers are not part of the demand curve.

items.q: Why does the supply curve slope upward?
options: Buyers want more at higher prices
Sellers' costs fall as the price rises
A higher price makes it worthwhile for sellers to produce more, even as extra output gets costlier
A higher price attracts more buyers
Sellers make more units at low prices to keep their revenue up

why.correct: Producing more usually costs more per extra unit, and a higher price covers those costs and makes the extra output profitable, so quantity supplied rises with price.
options: Buyers want less at higher prices; supply describes sellers.
Sellers' costs do not fall because the price rose.
Right: a higher price covers the cost of extra output.
Buyers are part of demand, not supply.
At a lower price, producing extra units is less worthwhile, so the quantity supplied falls; that is why supply slopes up.

items.q: Why does GDP measured by adding up spending on final goods equal GDP measured by adding up incomes?
options: Imports are added to income and subtracted from spending in the accounts
Each dollar spent on final goods is income to someone as a factor payment
The government sets total incomes equal to total spending each year by law
Profit is left out of both totals, so they match
Households spend their whole income, so saving in the economy is zero

why.correct: Spending, income and value added are three ways of measuring the same production: one person's spending is another's income.
options: Imports are subtracted in the expenditure approach; they are not added to anyone's income at home.
Right: the circular flow shows spending on output returning to households as factor income, so the two totals match.
No one sets them equal; they match because a purchase is income to the seller and, through the firm, to the owners of the factors.
Profit is income to the owners of firms and is counted in the income total; it is part of why spending and income match.
Households do save; spending and income are equal because each sale is someone's income, not because saving is zero.

items.q: An engineer who is a citizen of Country X works all year in Country Z. Her output is counted in
options: the GDP of Country Z
the GDP of Country X
the GDP of whichever country collects her income tax
the GDP of both countries
the GDP of neither country, because she is abroad

why.correct: The "domestic" in gross domestic product means inside the country's borders.
options: Right: GDP measures production inside a country's borders, whoever does it.
GDP is about where production happens, not the worker's citizenship.
GDP counts output produced inside a country's borders, whoever produces it; where her taxes go does not change that.
Counting it in both would double count one person's production.
Her work produces services in Country Z, so it is part of Country Z's GDP.

items.q: Two countries have the same GDP per capita. Which difference between them would GDP per capita fail to show?
options: One has much cleaner air and longer life spans than the other
One has twice the population and twice the total GDP
One produces more final goods per person than the other
One has a larger total market value of final output
One's residents earn a higher average income from production

why.correct: GDP per capita measures market output per person. Health, leisure, the environment and how income is shared all matter to well-being and are left out.
options: Right: health, the environment and other parts of well-being are outside GDP.
Doubling both leaves GDP per capita the same, and total GDP shows the difference in size.
Then their GDP per capita would differ; it would not be the same.
A larger total is visible in total GDP.
Spending on final output is income to someone, so GDP per capita is also average income per person; with equal GDP per capita, average incomes match and the measure would show any gap.

items.q: Ivy works 10 hours a week at a store but wants full-time work. How does the way she is counted affect the unemployment rate as a measure of joblessness?
options: She counts as unemployed, so the rate overstates joblessness
She counts as outside the labor force, so the rate is unaffected
She counts as half employed and half unemployed
She counts as a discouraged worker, so the rate is unaffected
She counts as employed, so the rate understates unused labor

why.correct: Underemployed and discouraged workers both make the official unemployment rate a low reading of how much labor goes unused.
options: Anyone with paid work in the survey week counts as employed, even part-time.
She has a job, so she is in the labor force as employed.
The survey has no half categories: she is employed.
A discouraged worker has no job and has stopped looking; Ivy has a job, so the survey counts her as employed.
Right: part-time workers who want full-time jobs are underemployed but counted as employed.

items.q: Based on the table, what is Vorland's unemployment rate?

why.correct: The labor force is the employed plus the unemployed, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>228</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>240</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">228 + 12 = 240</annotation></semantics></math> million, so the unemployment rate is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>12</mn><mn>240</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{12}{240} \times 100 = 5\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: That divides by the whole adult population, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>12</mn><mn>400</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{12}{400}</annotation></semantics></math>; the rate divides by the labor force, which leaves out the 160 million not in it.

Right: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>12</mn><mn>240</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{12}{240} \times 100 = 5\%</annotation></semantics></math>, with the labor force as the denominator.

That divides by the employed, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>12</mn><mn>228</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{12}{228}</annotation></semantics></math>; the labor force includes the unemployed too.

That is the labor force participation rate, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>240</mn><mn>400</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{240}{400} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>, not the unemployment rate.

That is the share of adults not in the labor force, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>160</mn><mn>400</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{160}{400} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>; they are neither employed nor unemployed.

items.q: Over a year, Sam's nominal wage rises 3% while the CPI rises 5%. What happens to his real wage?
options: It falls by about 8%
It rises by about 8%
It stays the same, because he got a raise
It falls by about 2%
It rises by about 3%

why.correct: Percent change in a real value is about the percent change in the nominal value minus the inflation rate: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3 - 5 = -2\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: The real wage changes by about the nominal change minus inflation: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\% - 5\% = -2\%</annotation></semantics></math>, not the two added together.
Price increases lower the real wage; they are not added to the raise.
A raise smaller than inflation still leaves him able to buy less.
Right: prices rose faster than his pay, so each hour of work buys about 2% less.
That is his nominal wage; the real wage also accounts for the 5% rise in prices.

items.q: A bank makes 30-year home loans at a fixed interest rate. Inflation then turns out far higher than the bank anticipated. Which statement best describes the result?
options: Homeowners repay in dollars worth less, so the bank loses
The bank gains, because homeowners have to pay more interest
Neither side is affected, because the rate was agreed to in advance
The bank gains, because the houses it lent against are worth more
Homeowners lose, because house prices rise with inflation

why.correct: Long fixed-rate contracts are where unanticipated inflation moves the most purchasing power. That risk is one reason lenders also offer adjustable rates.
options: Right: fixed-rate borrowers gain and the lender loses when inflation is higher than anticipated.
The rate is fixed, so homeowners pay the same dollar interest, which now buys less.
Agreeing in advance is what exposes both sides to the surprise.
The loan is repaid in a fixed number of dollars; a higher house price does not raise what the bank is paid, so surprise inflation hurts the lender.
Rising house prices add to homeowners' wealth; the fixed payments get easier, not harder.

items.q: How does the GDP deflator differ from the consumer price index?
options: It leaves out the prices of services
It measures the cost of a fixed basket bought by typical households
It is measured in dollars, not as an index
It includes the prices of imported consumer goods
It prices everything produced in the country, not a basket

why.correct: The deflator is a price index for everything in GDP; the CPI is a price index for a basket of consumer goods and services.
options: The deflator covers every final good and service produced in the country, services included.
That describes the CPI.
Both are indexes with a base year of 100.
Imports are not produced in the country, so they are outside GDP and its deflator; the CPI includes them.
Right: the deflator includes investment and government purchases and leaves out imports; the CPI prices what households buy, imports included.

items.q: Over many decades, Country Z's real GDP rises through several expansions and contractions. Which line best describes its potential output over that time?
options: A line that stays above real GDP in each year
A line that stays below real GDP in each year
A rising trend line that real GDP moves above and below
A flat line, because potential is fixed
A line that moves up and down with each expansion and contraction

why.correct: Real GDP fluctuates around potential output, which follows a long-term upward trend.
options: In booms real GDP rises above potential, so the gap is sometimes positive.
In contractions real GDP falls below potential, so potential output cannot sit below real GDP in every year.
Right: potential output grows over time, and the business cycle swings around it.
Potential grows as the labor force, capital and technology grow.
Actual real GDP swings; potential is the smoother trend.

items.q: The price level in Country Z falls while prices abroad stay the same. Through the exchange rate effect, what happens to Country Z's spending?
options: Its goods become cheaper relative to foreign goods, so net exports rise along AD
Its exports fall, because foreign buyers have less to spend
Its goods become dearer relative to foreign goods, so net exports fall
Imports rise because foreign goods are now cheaper for Country Z
AD shifts right because exports are a component of AD

why.correct: A lower domestic price level makes domestic goods relatively cheaper: exports rise, imports fall, and real GDP demanded rises along AD.
options: Right: exports rise and imports fall, so net exports and real GDP demanded rise, a movement down along AD.
Foreign incomes have not changed; a lower price level makes Country Z's goods cheaper abroad, so its exports rise.
A lower domestic price level makes domestic goods cheaper, not dearer, compared with foreign goods.
Foreign prices did not change while Country Z's fell, so foreign goods are relatively dearer and imports fall.
Exports rise here because Country Z's price level fell, so it is a movement along AD, not a shift.

items.q: Based on the table, what is the overall effect of the two changes on Country X's aggregate demand curve?
options: It shifts left, because investment fell by more than net exports rose
It shifts right, because exports rose while imports stayed the same
It does not shift, because consumption and government spending did not change
It moves along the curve to a lower price level and less output
It shifts right, because net exports rose by 20

why.correct: Total planned spending fell from 1,170 to 1,140 billion dollars at the same price level, so AD shifted left.
options: Right: investment fell by 50 and net exports rose by 20, so spending at the same price level fell by 30, a shift left.
Exports did rise by 20, but investment fell by 50 at the same time. Add both changes before deciding.
AD shifts when any component changes at a given price level, not only C or G. Investment and exports changed here.
The price level is unchanged in the table, so this is not a movement along AD. Spending changed for other reasons, which is a shift.
Net exports did rise by 20, but investment fell by 50, so total planned spending at each price level fell by 30.

items.q: A city gives a firm 1 million dollars to build a new stadium. Why can total spending in the economy rise by more than 1 million dollars?
options: Those who earn the million re-spend part of it, round after round
The firm's workers save the whole of their extra income
Prices rise, so each dollar of the stadium counts for more
The firm deposits the money in a bank, and the deposit counts as new spending
The government counts the stadium twice when measuring GDP

why.correct: The spending multiplier: new spending becomes someone's income, who spends the MPC share of it, and so on round after round.
options: Right: each round of income is partly re-spent, so the first million sets off more rounds of spending.
If every extra dollar were saved there would be no further rounds of spending, so total spending would rise by the first million alone.
The multiplier is about real output from rounds of re-spending, not about prices.
Saving is a leak from the rounds. It is the re-spending that multiplies.
GDP counts the stadium once. The extra comes from new spending by the people who earned the million.

items.q: Expected inflation rises across the economy: workers expect prices to rise faster next year, and they bargain for higher nominal wages now. What happens to SRAS?
options: It shifts right, because firms expect to sell at higher prices
It does not move, because nothing has happened to prices yet
The economy moves along SRAS to a higher price level
It shifts left, because firms' wage costs rise at every price level
LRAS shifts left, because workers expect to produce less

why.correct: When expected inflation rises, workers ask for higher nominal wages; that raises costs and shifts SRAS left.
options: Expecting higher prices raises wage demands, which raises costs; that shifts SRAS left.
Wages are bargained on what workers expect, so costs rise now.
A change in wages is a change in costs, which shifts the curve.
Right: what workers expect about prices feeds into wages, and higher wages shift SRAS left.
Expected inflation changes wage costs and so SRAS; it does not change the economy's capacity at full employment, which sets LRAS.

items.q: Which event could have caused the shift shown in the graph, from SRAS1 to SRAS2?
options: A new technology that lets workers produce more each hour
A fall in household wealth that cuts consumption
A government subsidy paid to firms for each unit they produce
A sharp rise in the price of energy used by most firms
A rise in the price level that lets firms charge more

why.correct: SRAS2 lies to the left of SRAS1: at each price level firms supply less, as when an input such as energy gets dearer.
options: Higher productivity lowers costs and shifts SRAS right, not left.
A fall in consumption shifts AD left; it does not move SRAS.
A subsidy lowers firms' costs and shifts SRAS right.
Right: higher energy prices raise production costs at every price level, so SRAS shifts left.
A change in the price level is a movement along SRAS, not a shift of the curve.

items.q: Full-employment real GDP in Country N is 800 billion dollars. Where does Country N's LRAS curve stand?
options: Vertical at the price level where AD meets SRAS
Horizontal at the current price level
Vertical at a real GDP of 800 billion dollars
Sloping up through 800 billion dollars
Vertical at whatever real GDP the economy produces this year

why.correct: LRAS stands at potential output (YF), here 800 billion dollars, whatever the price level.
options: LRAS stands at full-employment real GDP on the horizontal axis; it is not placed at a price level.
LRAS is vertical, not horizontal: output, not the price level, is fixed in the long run.
Right: LRAS is vertical at full-employment output.
An upward slope describes SRAS. In the long run the curve is vertical.
Actual output can be above or below full employment. LRAS stands at full-employment output.

items.q: An economy's AD and SRAS cross at a real GDP of 1,200 billion dollars, and LRAS is at 1,150 billion dollars. Which describes the economy?
options: A recessionary gap of 50 billion dollars, with unemployment below the natural rate
A recessionary gap of 50 billion dollars, with unemployment above the natural rate
An inflationary gap of 50 billion dollars, with unemployment above the natural rate
Long-run equilibrium, because AD and SRAS cross
An inflationary gap of 50 billion dollars, with unemployment below the natural rate

why.correct: Real GDP 1,200 > full-employment 1,150: an inflationary (positive) gap of 50 billion dollars, unemployment below the natural rate.
options: Output above LRAS is an inflationary gap, not a recessionary one; unemployment is below the natural rate there.
Output is above potential, not below it.
Above-potential output needs more workers, so unemployment is below the natural rate.
The crossing is 50 billion to the right of LRAS, so the economy is not at long-run equilibrium.
Right: output exceeds potential by 50 billion, so firms are hiring beyond full employment.

items.q: A rise in interest rates at an unchanged price level leads firms to cancel plans for new equipment. What happens in the short run?
options: SRAS shifts left: the price level rises and real GDP falls
AD shifts left: the price level rises and real GDP falls
AD shifts left: the price level falls, real GDP falls and unemployment rises
AD shifts left: the price level falls and unemployment falls
AD shifts right: firms have more cash to spend on other things

why.correct: Less investment at every price level shifts AD left: lower price level, lower real GDP, higher unemployment.
options: Investment is spending, which is AD. Firms' production costs today did not change.
A leftward AD shift lowers both the price level and real GDP; a higher price level with lower output comes from SRAS shifting left.
Right: less investment is a negative demand shock.
Lower output means fewer jobs, so unemployment rises.
Canceled investment is less spending, which shifts AD left.

items.q: In the long run, what is the effect of a lasting rise in aggregate demand, starting from full employment?
options: A higher price level and higher real GDP
The same price level with higher real GDP
A lower price level with real GDP back at full employment
The original price level with real GDP back at full employment
A higher price level with real GDP back at full-employment output

why.correct: In the long run, AD changes affect the price level but not real GDP: output returns to LRAS.
options: That is the short run. In the long run wages rise and output returns to YF.
In the long run output is set by LRAS; more spending only raises prices.
The long-run adjustment from an inflationary gap raises the price level further.
Nominal wages rise and SRAS shifts left, so output returns to full employment at a higher price level, not the old one.
Right: wages catch up and SRAS shifts left, so only the price level stays higher.

items.q: The graph shows Tavor's economy. If neither the government nor the central bank acts, what happens in the long run?
options: Spending recovers, AD shifts right, and output returns to full employment at a higher price level
Nominal wages rise, SRAS shifts left, and output returns to full employment at a higher price level
Nominal wages fall, SRAS shifts right, and output returns to full employment at a lower price level
LRAS shifts left to the current level of output, and the price level stays the same
Output stays below full employment, because prices in the economy are sticky

why.correct: Output is below full employment (left of LRAS), so unemployment is above the natural rate. Over time nominal wages and other input prices fall, SRAS shifts right, and the economy returns to full-employment output at a lower price level.
options: Self-adjustment works through wages and SRAS; a recovery in spending would be a separate shift of AD, not the long-run mechanism.
That is the adjustment from an inflationary gap; here output is below full employment, so wages fall rather than rise.
Right: with output below LRAS, falling wages and input prices shift SRAS right until it meets AD on LRAS.
LRAS is set by resources and technology; a gap does not move it.
Wages and prices are slow to adjust in the short run, but in the long run they do adjust, which closes the gap.

items.q: It takes a year to notice a recession, pass a spending bill and start the projects. Why can this delay make fiscal policy less effective?
options: The economy may already be recovering when the spending arrives
The spending is counted in GDP once the bill passes, not when it is spent
A delay lowers the MPC, so the multiplier shrinks by the time money is spent
Spending that arrives late shifts SRAS instead of AD
Delayed spending is not counted in GDP

why.correct: Fiscal policy has lags (recognizing the problem, deciding, carrying it out). If the economy recovers in the meantime, the stimulus can overshoot into an inflationary gap.
options: Right: these lags mean policy can hit at the wrong point in the cycle.
GDP counts spending when the goods and services are produced; the problem is timing, since the money may arrive after the gap has closed.
The MPC does not depend on how long a bill takes to pass.
Government purchases shift AD whenever they arrive.
Government purchases count in GDP in the year they happen.

items.q: Pellara's economy has a recessionary gap of $200 billion, and its MPC is 0.75. Ignoring any effect on prices, how must government purchases change to close the gap?
options: A decrease of $50 billion
An increase of $200 billion
An increase of $800 billion
An increase of about $66.7 billion
An increase of $50 billion

why.correct: The spending multiplier is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{1 - 0.75} = 4</annotation></semantics></math>. A recessionary gap needs more spending, and the change is the gap divided by the multiplier: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>200</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{200}{4} = 50</annotation></semantics></math> billion dollars.
options: Cutting purchases shifts AD left and widens a recessionary gap; closing it needs more spending.

Spending 200 billion would raise output by <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>800</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">200 \times 4 = 800</annotation></semantics></math> billion through the multiplier; divide the gap by the multiplier.
That multiplies the gap by the multiplier; the change needed is the gap divided by it.

That divides by the tax multiplier, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>0.75</mn><mn>0.25</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{0.75}{0.25} = 3</annotation></semantics></math>, the answer for a tax cut; government purchases use the spending multiplier, 4.

Right: purchases rise by <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>200</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{200}{4} = 50</annotation></semantics></math> billion dollars, and the multiplier turns that into 200 billion of output.

items.q: Country S replaces its progressive income tax with one tax of the same fixed dollar amount per household, whatever the income. How does this change the economy's response to a fall in AD?
options: Disposable income falls by more, so recessions get deeper
Disposable income falls by less, so recessions get milder
Tax collections rise in the downturn, so AD shifts right
Nothing changes, because tax collections are the same on average
SRAS shifts right faster, so the economy adjusts sooner

why.correct: A tax that does not change with income is not an automatic stabilizer, so swings in income pass straight through to spending.
options: Right: a fixed tax does not fall when incomes fall, so it no longer cushions spending.
A fixed tax stays the same as income falls, so it removes the cushion.
A fixed tax per household does not change with income, so collections stay the same in a downturn; nothing pushes AD right.
What matters is how collections change over the cycle; a fixed tax does not move.
The tax change works on disposable income and AD, not on wages and SRAS.

items.q: A company sells new bonds to pay for a new factory. In economic terms, what is the company doing?
options: Borrowing from the people who buy the bonds
Selling ownership shares to new investors
Lending money to the bond buyers
Creating new money to pay for the factory
Saving part of its profit for later

why.correct: Firms finance investment either by borrowing (bonds, loans) or by selling ownership (stock).
options: Right: selling bonds is borrowing; the company will pay interest and repay the buyers.
Selling ownership shares is issuing stock. Bonds are borrowing.
The money flows to the company; the buyers are the lenders, not the borrowers.
Selling bonds creates no new money; the company borrows money that already exists from the people who buy the bonds and promises to repay it with interest.
The company raises outside money by borrowing; it is not saving its own profit.

items.q: Which asset is the least liquid?
options: A $20 bill in a wallet
A checking account balance
A savings account balance
A rental house
A government bond

why.correct: The longer and costlier it is to turn an asset into spendable money at full value, the less liquid it is.
options: Currency is money itself, the most liquid asset there is.
A checking balance can be spent by card or check right away.
Savings can be moved to checking or withdrawn quickly at full value.
Right: selling a house takes weeks and its price is uncertain, so it is the least liquid.
A bond can be sold quickly in the bond market, so it is more liquid than a house, which takes weeks and fees to sell.

items.q: Why do economists say a firm deciding whether to borrow for new equipment cares about the real interest rate?
options: The real rate is the rate written on the loan
Lenders ignore inflation when they set rates
The real rate is set by the government each year
It measures the true cost of borrowing in buying power
The real rate is the same as the nominal rate

why.correct: Borrowing decisions depend on the real interest rate, the cost of borrowing after inflation.
options: The written rate is the nominal rate.
Lenders do build the expected inflation rate into nominal rates.
Lenders and borrowers set loan rates; the real rate is the nominal rate minus the expected inflation rate.
Right: with inflation, the firm's prices and revenue rise too, so the real rate is the true cost.
The two differ by expected inflation; they are equal when expected inflation is zero, which is not the general case.

items.q: Which loan term would have protected the bank from this surprise?
options: A fixed nominal rate agreed before the surprise
A longer repayment period
A lower fixed nominal rate
A smaller down payment from Sam
A nominal rate that adjusts with inflation

why.correct: Adjustable or inflation-linked rates move with inflation, so a surprise does not shift buying power from lender to borrower.
options: A fixed nominal rate is what left the bank exposed: when inflation came in above what was expected, the real rate it earned fell.
A longer loan at a fixed rate exposes the bank to more years of surprise inflation.
A lower fixed rate would leave the bank with an even lower real return.
The down payment changes the loan size, not how inflation changes the real return.
Right: a variable rate that rises with inflation keeps the real rate close to what was agreed.

items.q: In a barter economy, a plumber who wants shoes has to find a shoemaker who wants plumbing. What problem of barter does money solve here?
options: The need for a double coincidence of wants
The problem of inflation
The need to produce more goods
The problem of scarcity
The difficulty of saving for the future

why.correct: As a medium of exchange, money removes the need for each trade to match two people's wants exactly.
options: Right: with money, the plumber sells plumbing to anyone and buys shoes from anyone.
Barter has no money prices to inflate; the problem is matching wants.
Money does not create goods; it makes trading them easier.
Money does not end scarcity; resources are still limited.
Saving is about money as a store of value; the plumber's problem is trading today, which money as a medium of exchange solves.

items.q: What gives fiat money, such as a modern dollar bill, its value?
options: The gold the government keeps for each bill
The paper and ink it is printed with
Its use as a good in production
Government decree and people's willingness to accept it
The bank deposits that back each bill

why.correct: Fiat money has value because the government declares it money and people accept it in trade.
options: Modern currencies are not backed by gold.
The materials are worth a few cents, far less than the bill.
That describes commodity money, such as salt or gold, which is valued as a good.
Right: it is legal tender and people trust others to take it.
Fiat money is backed by no commodity or deposit; its value rests on government decree and people's willingness to accept it.

items.q: The required reserve ratio is 0.1. A customer withdraws $1,000 in cash from her checking account. How do the bank's excess reserves change?
options: They rise by $100
They fall by $1,000
They fall by $100
They do not change
They fall by $900

why.correct: A withdrawal lowers reserves by its full amount and required reserves by the ratio times that amount; excess falls by the difference.
options: Required reserves fall by $100, but reserves fall by the full $1,000, so excess reserves fall by <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>900</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1{,}000 - 100 = 900</annotation></semantics></math> dollars.
Reserves fall by $1,000, but required reserves also fall by $100, so excess falls by $900.
$100 is the drop in required reserves. Excess reserves fall by $1,000 - $100.
Cash paid out comes from reserves, so excess reserves fall.
Right: reserves fall $1,000 and required reserves fall $100 (10% of the smaller deposits).

items.q: The required reserve ratio is 0.2, and the bank in the table holds no other deposits. In this limited-reserves banking system, what is the largest possible increase in the money supply if the bank lends out its excess reserves?

why.correct: Required reserves are <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>500</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>0.2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">500 \times 0.2 = 100</annotation></semantics></math> dollars, so excess reserves are <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>150</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150 - 100 = 50</annotation></semantics></math> dollars. The money multiplier is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>0.2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{0.2} = 5</annotation></semantics></math>, so lending them out can raise the money supply by at most <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>250</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50 \times 5 = 250</annotation></semantics></math> dollars.
options: That multiplies total deposits; the new money comes from the $50 of excess reserves.
The bank can lend $50, but as the loans are deposited and lent again the whole system creates more; multiply by the money multiplier.
That multiplies total reserves; only the $50 of excess reserves can be lent.
Right: excess reserves of $50 times the money multiplier of 5 is $250.
$100 is the required reserves the bank has to keep, not the new money it can create.

items.q: In the money market, the nominal interest rate is above equilibrium. How does the market move back to equilibrium?
options: People hold more money than they want, sell bonds, and the rate rises
People want more money, sell bonds, and the rate rises
The central bank lowers the money supply until the rate matches
People hold more money than they want, buy bonds, and the rate falls
The central bank raises the money supply until the rate matches

why.correct: A surplus of money leads people to buy bonds: bond prices rise and interest rates fall until people want to hold the money that exists.
options: With surplus money, people buy bonds, which lowers the rate.
Above equilibrium people want less money than exists, not more.
The market adjusts through bond buying; the supply does not have to change.
Right: buying bonds raises bond prices, which lowers interest rates.
The market moves back by itself: people buy bonds with the money they do not want to hold, bond prices rise and the rate falls.

items.q: A central bank that operates with limited reserves lowers the discount rate. What happens to the money supply and interest rates?
options: The money supply falls and interest rates rise
The money supply falls and interest rates fall
Neither changes, since the discount rate is a fee
The money supply rises and interest rates rise
The money supply rises and interest rates fall

why.correct: The discount rate is what the central bank charges banks for loans of reserves; lowering it is expansionary.
options: Cheaper borrowing from the central bank adds reserves, which raises the money supply.
A lower discount rate makes borrowing reserves cheaper, so banks lend more and the money supply rises, not falls.
The discount rate is the cost of borrowing reserves, so it changes bank lending.
More money lowers the nominal interest rate on the money market.
Right: banks borrow more reserves, lend more, and the money supply rises.

items.q: Nimbra's central bank operates with ample reserves. Which action could cause the change shown in the graph, and what is its short-run effect on real GDP?
options: Raising the interest rate on reserve balances; real GDP falls
Raising the interest rate on reserve balances; real GDP rises
Selling bonds to cut the supply of reserves; real GDP falls
Lowering the interest rate on reserve balances; real GDP falls
Raising the required reserve ratio; real GDP rises

why.correct: With ample reserves the central bank moves the policy rate by setting its administered rates: raising interest on reserve balances lifts the flat part of reserve demand, so the policy rate rises. Other interest rates follow, investment and consumption fall, AD shifts left and real GDP falls.
options: Right: a higher administered rate raises the policy rate, so borrowing falls, AD shifts left and real GDP falls.
A higher policy rate makes borrowing costlier, so investment and AD fall; real GDP falls, not rises.
Reserve supply did not move in the graph; with ample reserves the rate is moved by the administered rate, not by the quantity of reserves.
Lowering the administered rate would lower the flat part of reserve demand and the policy rate; the graph shows it rising.
A reserve requirement is a limited-reserves tool, and a tighter policy lowers real GDP rather than raising it.

items.q: Why does the supply of loanable funds slope upward?
options: A higher real interest rate makes borrowers want more funds
A higher real rate rewards saving, so people save more
Banks are required to lend more when rates rise
Inflation rises as the real interest rate rises
The government saves more when interest rates rise

why.correct: Saving responds to the reward for saving, the real interest rate: a higher rate brings out more loanable funds.
options: Borrowers want fewer funds at a higher rate, which is why demand slopes down; supply slopes up because savers lend more.
Right: the real rate is the reward for saving.
No rule makes banks lend more; savers choose to supply more at higher rates.
The real rate already removes inflation; the slope comes from savers' choices.
Public saving depends on taxes and spending, not on the slope of supply.

items.q: Which statement correctly compares fiscal and monetary policy in the short run?
options: Fiscal policy shifts AD; monetary policy shifts SRAS through interest costs
Monetary policy shifts AD in limited reserves but LRAS in ample reserves
Both shift AD; fiscal policy works through spending or taxes, monetary policy through interest rates
Both shift LRAS by changing how much the economy can produce
Both shift SRAS; fiscal policy through taxes, monetary policy through wages

why.correct: Fiscal and monetary policy are both stabilization tools that shift AD; they differ in the first links of their chains.
options: Interest rates change borrowing and spending, so monetary policy shifts AD.
The framework changes the tool and the graph, not the curve the policy shifts.
Right: each is a demand-side tool, with a different first link in the chain.
Stabilization policy aims at spending in the short run; LRAS depends on resources and technology.
In the short run both work on demand: spending, taxes and interest rates change AD, not SRAS.

items.q: In Bela, which variable's change cannot be determined without knowing the sizes of the two policies?
options: Real output
Aggregate demand
Interest rates on loans
The price level
The unemployment rate

why.correct: Two expansionary policies give a clear AD effect; their effects on loan rates point opposite ways. (Bela's policy rate itself falls, because it follows the administered rate.)
options: Both policies raise AD, so real output rises in the short run.
Both actions in Bela are expansionary, so AD rises for sure; the interest rate is the variable the two push in opposite directions.
Right: higher spending pushes loan rates up while the lower administered rate pulls them down.
Both policies raise AD, so the price level rises.
Higher output means firms hire more, so unemployment falls.

items.q: A new technology sharply lowers energy costs for firms (a positive supply shock). What happens on the Phillips curve graph in the short run?
options: The SRPC shifts right: inflation and unemployment both rise
The economy moves down along the SRPC: inflation falls and unemployment rises
The economy moves up along the SRPC: inflation rises and unemployment falls
LRPC shifts right: the natural rate of unemployment rises
The SRPC shifts left: inflation and unemployment both fall

why.correct: A positive supply shock is the mirror image of a negative one: SRAS right, SRPC left.
options: That is a negative supply shock, such as a rise in oil prices.
A movement along the SRPC comes from a change in AD; a supply shock shifts the SRPC itself, here to the left.
A movement along the SRPC comes from a change in AD.
Cheaper energy does not raise the natural rate; the short-run curve moves.
Right: SRAS shifts right, so the price level rises more slowly and output rises; inflation and unemployment fall together.

items.q: What does the vertical long-run Phillips curve show?
options: In the long run, higher inflation keeps unemployment permanently lower
In the long run, the inflation rate is fixed whatever the unemployment rate
In the long run, unemployment is at the natural rate at any inflation rate
In the long run, unemployment falls to zero when inflation is high enough
In the long run, inflation and unemployment rise and fall together

why.correct: LRPC is the Phillips curve version of LRAS: both are vertical at full employment, where unemployment equals the natural rate.
options: That is the short-run trade-off. It disappears once expected inflation catches up.
A fixed inflation rate would be a horizontal line. LRPC fixes unemployment, not inflation.
Right: once expectations adjust there is no lasting trade-off, so LRPC is vertical at the natural rate.
Frictional and structural unemployment remain at any inflation rate; that is the natural rate.
The vertical LRPC says unemployment is at the natural rate whatever inflation is: no long-run link at all, not a positive one.

items.q: Which event could cause the change shown in the graph?
options: A rise in aggregate demand
A rise in the inflation rate that workers and firms expect
A fall in the natural rate of unemployment
A new technology that cuts firms' costs
A fall in aggregate demand

why.correct: The short-run Phillips curve shifted right: at each unemployment rate, inflation is higher. A rise in expected inflation (or an adverse supply shock) does this; changes in aggregate demand move the economy along the curve.
options: A change in AD moves the economy along the SRPC; it does not shift the curve.
Right: when expected inflation rises, wages and prices rise faster at each unemployment rate, so the SRPC shifts right.
A change in the natural rate shifts the LRPC, which did not move in the graph.
Lower costs are a positive supply shock, which shifts the SRPC left, not right.
A fall in AD is a movement down along the SRPC, to lower inflation and higher unemployment.

items.q: Why can a rise in the money supply raise real GDP in the short run but not in the long run?
options: In the long run, the money supply returns to its old level by itself
Velocity doubles in the short run and then falls to zero
Nominal wages and some prices adjust slowly, so output can rise until they catch up
The central bank takes the money back out in the long run
LRAS shifts right in the short run and back left in the long run

why.correct: In the short run money is not neutral because of sticky wages and prices; in the long run it is.
options: Nothing removes the new money; output returns to full employment because wages and prices adjust up, leaving a higher price level.
The quantity theory treats velocity as roughly steady; it does not swing like this.
Right: sticky wages let a rise in AD raise output in the short run; once wages adjust, SRAS shifts left and output returns to full employment.
The money supply stays higher; it is the wage adjustment that removes the output gain.
LRAS depends on resources and technology, not on the money supply.

items.q: Lenders in Kaldo come to expect this high inflation. What happens to the nominal interest rates they charge on new loans?
options: They fall, because there is more money available to lend
They fall, because loans will be repaid in more valuable money
They stay the same, because the real interest rate is unchanged
They rise, because lenders add expected inflation to the real return they want
They fall to zero, because money loses value too quickly to lend

why.correct: Nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation. Expected inflation shows up in nominal interest rates.
options: More money does not lower nominal rates for long when lenders expect prices to rise fast; they need compensation for it.
High expected inflation means money will be worth less when loans are repaid, so lenders raise nominal rates.
An unchanged real rate means the nominal rate rises one for one with expected inflation.
Right: the nominal rate is roughly the real rate plus expected inflation, so higher expected inflation means higher nominal rates.
Lenders keep lending but demand a higher nominal rate to cover inflation.

items.q: In Halden, the velocity of money and real output stay the same while the money supply doubles. According to the quantity theory of money, what happens in the long run?
options: Nominal GDP stays the same, because real output is unchanged
Real output doubles
The price level stays the same, because velocity is unchanged
The price level rises by half
The price level doubles

why.correct: In <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M \times V = P \times Y</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> unchanged, doubling <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> doubles <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M \times V</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P \times Y</annotation></semantics></math> doubles; with <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> fixed, the price level <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> doubles.
options: Nominal GDP is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P \times Y</annotation></semantics></math>, which equals <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M \times V</annotation></semantics></math>; it doubles, because the price level doubles.
In the long run real output is set by resources and technology; the question also holds it unchanged.
Velocity being unchanged is why the whole rise in money shows up in nominal GDP, and so in the price level.

With <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> fixed, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> changes in proportion to <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>: doubling money doubles the price level.
Right: with velocity and real output fixed, the price level moves in proportion to the money supply.

items.q: Interest rates on new government bonds rise. With no change in tax law or programs, what happens to the deficit over the next few years?
options: It shrinks, because higher rates bring the government more revenue
It grows, because interest on the debt is part of government outlays
It stays the same, because interest is not part of the budget
It disappears, because higher rates lower the price of existing bonds
It shrinks, because higher rates cut spending on programs

why.correct: A larger debt or higher interest rates raise interest outlays, which add to the deficit.
options: The government pays interest on its bonds; it does not collect it.
Right: as old bonds are replaced at higher rates, interest payments and so outlays rise.
Interest on the debt is counted in government outlays.
Lower prices of existing bonds do not change what the government owes in interest.
The question holds programs unchanged; higher rates raise interest outlays, so the deficit grows.

items.q: Rastova's national debt was 2,000 billion dollars at the start of Year 1. Based on the table, what is the debt at the end of Year 3?
options: 2,130 billion dollars
2,150 billion dollars
2,170 billion dollars
1,870 billion dollars
130 billion dollars

why.correct: Each deficit adds to the debt and each surplus reduces it: deficits of 100 and 50 billion in Years 1 and 2, then a surplus of 20 billion in Year 3, so the debt is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2{,}000 + 100 + 50 - 20</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>130</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 2{,}130</annotation></semantics></math> billion dollars.
options: Right: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2{,}000 + 100 + 50 - 20</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>130</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 2{,}130</annotation></semantics></math> billion dollars.
That adds the two deficits but leaves out Year 3, when revenue exceeded outlays and the surplus paid down 20 billion.
Year 3 is a surplus, not a deficit: revenue of 1,020 is more than outlays of 1,000, so it lowers the debt.
Deficits add to the debt; subtracting them reverses the sign of the budget balance.
130 billion dollars is the net amount the government borrowed over the three years; the debt also includes the 2,000 billion owed at the start.

items.q: When is crowding out likely to be largest?
options: When the economy is in a deep recession and many firms have stopped borrowing to invest
When firms have many profitable projects and the government borrows nothing
When the government runs a budget surplus and repays its bonds
When the economy is at full employment and the supply of saving is not growing
When households save much more at the same time the government borrows

why.correct: Crowding out is strongest near full employment and weakest in a deep recession.
options: In a deep recession private demand for funds is weak, so government borrowing raises the real rate less.
Crowding out comes from government borrowing; with no new borrowing there is nothing to crowd private investment out.
A surplus lowers the demand for loanable funds; there is no borrowing to crowd anything out.
Right: with output at capacity, extra government borrowing mostly bids funds away from private borrowers, so the real rate rises a lot.
More saving pushes the real rate back down, which reduces crowding out.

items.q: Brisca's government borrows to pay for a budget deficit, as the graph shows. What happens to the real interest rate and to private investment spending?
options: The real interest rate falls, and private investment rises
The real interest rate rises, and private investment rises
The real interest rate rises, and private investment falls
The real interest rate stays the same, and private investment falls
The real interest rate falls, and private investment falls

why.correct: Government borrowing raises the demand for loanable funds, so the real interest rate rises. At the higher rate firms borrow less for new capital, so private investment falls: crowding out.
options: The demand for loanable funds rose, which raises the real interest rate rather than lowering it.
A higher real interest rate raises the cost of borrowing, so firms invest less, not more.
Right: the higher real interest rate makes borrowing for new capital costlier, so private investment falls.
The graph shows the equilibrium real interest rate rising as demand shifts right.
The real interest rate rises in the graph; investment falls because of that rise.

items.q: Why do economists say productivity is the key to a country's standard of living over time?
options: Real GDP per capita keeps rising for decades when output per worker keeps rising
Higher productivity raises the price level, which raises nominal incomes
Higher productivity raises the money supply, which raises spending
Productivity matters mainly in recessions, when it raises AD
Higher productivity shifts AD right, which raises output in the short run

why.correct: Productivity, output per worker or per hour, rises with physical capital, human capital and technology.
options: Right: the share of people working cannot rise forever, so lasting gains come from each worker producing more.
Productivity gains raise real output; they tend to hold prices down, not push them up.
The central bank sets the money supply; productivity sets capacity.
Productivity raises output per worker and LRAS year after year; it is a long-run supply story, not a recession fix.
Productivity is a supply-side change that shifts LRAS.

items.q: An economy at full employment raises transfer payments to households. What is the main effect, and on which curve?
options: AD shifts right: the price level rises, with little lasting output gain
LRAS shifts right, so potential output rises and the PPC shifts outward
SRAS shifts right, so the price level falls
The money supply rises, so the real interest rate falls
AD shifts left, so output falls

why.correct: Policies that raise spending shift AD; only those that raise capacity shift LRAS.
options: Right: transfers raise disposable income and spending, but at full employment they mostly push up prices; they do not add capacity.
Transfers raise spending, not capital, skills or technology.
Transfers do not lower firms' costs.
Transfers are fiscal policy and do not change the money supply; their main effect is on consumption and AD.
More transfers raise spending, shifting AD right.

items.q: Arland's exports fall, while its imports, income and transfers stay the same. With nothing else changing, which is most likely?
options: Its current account balance falls and its capital and financial account balance rises by the same amount
Both balances fall by the same amount
Its current account balance stays the same, because imports did not change
Its current account balance rises, because fewer goods leave the country
Its government's budget balance falls by the amount exports fell

why.correct: The current account balance falls; the capital and financial account balance rises by the same amount.
options: Right: lower exports lower the current account balance; to pay for the same imports Arland must sell more assets abroad or borrow more, so the capital and financial account balance rises by the same amount.
The two balances sum to zero, so they move in opposite directions.
Exports are part of the current account, so a fall in exports lowers the balance.
Exports are a credit in the current account, so fewer exports lower the current account balance.
Exports are sales by Arland residents to foreigners; they are not government revenue or outlays.

items.q: The rate moves from 2 bels per arl to 2.5 bels per arl. Student A says: "Bels per arl rose, so the arl got stronger." Student B says: "Arls per bel fell, so the bel got weaker." Who is right?
options: Student A, but Student B has the direction backward
Student B, but Student A has the direction backward
Both: they describe one change from its two sides
Student A, while Student B describes a different change
Neither: a higher rate means a weaker currency

why.correct: Appreciation of one currency is depreciation of the other.
options: Student B is also right: arls per bel fell from 0.5 to 0.4, so the bel buys less of an arl.
Student A is also right: each arl buys more bels, so the arl appreciated.
Right: an arl appreciation and a bel depreciation are the same change. Bels per arl rose from 2 to 2.5; arls per bel fell from 0.5 to 0.4.
Both students describe the same move from its two sides: when the arl buys more bels, each bel buys fewer arls.
In a bels-per-arl quote, a higher number means each arl buys more, so the arl is stronger.

items.q: Arland residents increase their purchases of Belvian goods. What changes in the two currency markets?
options: Demand for arls falls, and supply of bels falls
Demand for arls rises, and supply of bels rises
Supply of arls falls, and demand for bels falls
Supply of arls rises, and demand for bels rises
Supply of arls rises, and the bel market does not change

why.correct: Arls offered for bels: supply of arls right, demand for bels right. The arl depreciates and the bel appreciates.
options: Arland buyers need bels to pay Belvian sellers, so they supply arls and demand bels; neither of these falls.
Arland residents are buying bels with arls, not the other way round.
More purchases of Belvian goods mean more arls offered and more bels wanted.
Right: one set of trades, arls sold for bels, appears as more supply in the arl market and more demand in the bel market.
Every arl sold for bels is a bel bought, so the bel market shows the mirror change.

items.q: The graph shows a change in the market for Talmia's currency, the tal, which trades for Sarvel's currency, the sarv. Which event could cause the change?
options: Incomes in Sarvel rise
Talmia residents buy more goods made in Sarvel
Real interest rates in Talmia rise
Sarvel residents buy fewer goods made in Talmia
Talmia's price level falls relative to Sarvel's

why.correct: The demand for tals shifted left, so the tal depreciates. Demand for tals comes from people in Sarvel who buy Talmia's goods and assets; if they buy fewer Talmia goods, they want fewer tals at each exchange rate.
options: Higher incomes in Sarvel raise its purchases of Talmia's goods, so the demand for tals rises.
Talmia residents who buy more from Sarvel supply more tals; that shifts the supply curve, not demand.
Higher real interest rates in Talmia draw financial capital in, which raises the demand for tals.
Right: fewer purchases of Talmia's goods by Sarvel residents mean less demand for tals.
Cheaper Talmia goods raise Sarvel's purchases of them, which raises the demand for tals.

items.q: Arland's central bank works in a limited-reserves framework and buys government bonds on the open market. What happens to the arl, other things equal?
options: It appreciates, because the money supply in Arland rises
It appreciates, because the central bank is buying
It depreciates, because Arland interest rates fall
It does not change, because bond purchases are domestic
It depreciates, because Arland inflation falls

why.correct: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, so the currency depreciates.
options: More money and lower Arland interest rates make Arland assets less attractive, so demand for arls falls and the arl depreciates.
Buying bonds adds reserves and money, which lowers interest rates; lower rates make Arland assets less attractive.
Right: in a limited-reserves system, buying bonds raises the money supply and lowers interest rates, so Arland assets pay less, demand for arls falls and supply rises.
The purchases change Arland interest rates, and those rates affect what foreign and Arland savers want to buy.
Expansionary monetary policy would, if anything, raise inflation; the short-run link here is lower interest rates.

items.q: Which Arland business is most likely hurt when the arl appreciates against the bel?
options: A winery that sells most of its wine in Belvia, priced in arls
A store that imports clothes from Belvia, priced in bels
A firm that owes a loan payable in bels
An Arland travel agency selling trips to Belvia to Arland residents
An Arland family planning a holiday in Belvia

why.correct: An appreciation hurts exporters: their goods cost more abroad.
options: Right: its wine now costs Belvian buyers more bels, so it sells less abroad.
Each arl buys more bels, so its imported clothes cost it fewer arls: it gains.
Each arl buys more bels, so the loan takes fewer arls to repay.
Trips to Belvia, priced in bels, are now cheaper for Arland travelers, so the agency sells more of them.
A stronger arl buys more bels, so a holiday in Belvia gets cheaper for the family; they gain from the appreciation.

items.q: Bonds in Arland pay a nominal rate of 7% with expected inflation of 4%. Bonds in Belvia pay 5% with expected inflation of 1%. Other things equal, which way does financial capital tend to flow?
options: Into Arland, because 7% is the higher of the two nominal rates
Into Belvia, because its real interest rate is higher
Into Arland, because its real interest rate is higher
Into Arland, because its inflation is higher
Neither way, because both pay a positive rate

why.correct: Real rates: Arland 3%, Belvia 4%. Capital flows toward the higher real rate.
options: Savers compare real returns: Arland pays 7 - 4 = 3 percent real, Belvia 5 - 1 = 4 percent real.
Right: the real rate is 3 percent in Arland and 4 percent in Belvia, so savers move toward Belvia even though Arland's nominal rate is higher.

Arland's real rate is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>%</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7\% - 4\% = 3\%</annotation></semantics></math> and Belvia's is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>%</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\% - 1\% = 4\%</annotation></semantics></math>, so Belvia's real rate is the higher one.
Higher expected inflation lowers the real return, which makes Arland less attractive, not more.
Funds move toward the higher real return, and the two real rates differ.

items.q: A city council spends this year's budget on a new bridge, so it repairs fewer school buildings. What is this an example of?
options: A command economy
Economic growth
An increase in resources
A choice with nothing given up
A trade-off

why.correct: Choosing more of one thing means less of another: a trade-off.
options: A city budget choice happens in every economic system.
Growth would raise what the city can do in total; here a fixed budget went to one use and another was given up, a trade-off.
The budget did not grow; it was divided.
School repairs were given up.
Right: the bridge comes at the cost of school repairs.

items.q: Why is a production possibilities curve usually bowed outward rather than straight?
options: Each resource is equally good at making both goods
Some resources are better at making one good than the other
The economy has idle resources at each point
The economy produces at a point inside the curve
Prices rise as output rises

why.correct: As an economy makes more of one good, it must use resources less and less suited to it, so each extra unit costs more of the other good.
options: Equally suited resources would give a straight line.
Right: specialized resources create increasing opportunity cost.
Idle resources put the economy inside the curve; they do not shape it.
A point inside the curve means unused resources; it says nothing about why the curve itself is bowed.
The PPC shows quantities that can be produced, not prices.

items.q: Which pair of goods are complements?
options: Butter and margarine
Hot dogs and hot dog buns
Train tickets and bus tickets
Coffee and tea
Paper books and e-books

why.correct: Complements are used together, so a higher price of one lowers demand for the other.
options: They replace each other: substitutes.
Right: they are bought and used together.
They replace each other: substitutes.
Coffee and tea are substitutes: a rise in the price of one raises the demand for the other. Complements are used together.
They replace each other: substitutes.

items.q: Honey makers expect the price of honey to rise sharply next month. What happens to the supply of honey this month?
options: Demand for honey decreases this month
It increases, because makers rush to produce more honey
The quantity supplied rises along the curve this month
It is unchanged until the price actually rises
It decreases, because makers hold back jars to sell later at the higher price

why.correct: Expectations are a determinant of supply. Expecting a higher price later, sellers offer less now: today's supply shifts left.
options: The makers' expectations shift supply; and buyers who expect a higher price would buy more now, not less.
Producing more takes time; the jars on hand are held back for the higher price.
Today's price has not changed, so there is no movement along the curve.
Expectations shift supply before the price changes.
Right: sellers store jars for next month.

items.q: Cold weather arrives, and buyers now want 30 more cups at every price in the table. What is the new equilibrium price?

why.correct: The new quantities demanded are 120, 105, 90, 75 and 60. At $4, 75 cups are demanded and 75 supplied.
options: At $3, 90 would now be demanded but only 60 supplied.
At $5, 90 would be supplied but only 60 demanded.
At $1 the new quantity demanded is 120 cups and the quantity supplied 30, a shortage, not an equilibrium.
At $2, 105 would be demanded but only 45 supplied.
Right: 75 demanded and 75 supplied at $4.

items.q: A furniture maker builds 100 chairs this year but sells only 80. How do the 20 unsold chairs enter this year's GDP?
options: They are not counted until a household buys them
As exports, because they leave the factory
As consumption, because chairs are consumer goods
As government purchases
As investment, an addition to inventory

why.correct: Inventory changes are part of investment. That keeps GDP a measure of production: output made this year is counted this year, whether or not it has been sold.
options: GDP counts production in the year it happens. When the chairs sell next year, inventory falls by the same amount, so they are not counted twice.
Exports are sales to buyers abroad; chairs made this year and not yet sold are counted as investment in inventory.
Nobody has consumed them yet; unsold output goes into inventory investment.
No government bought the chairs.
Right: goods produced and not yet sold are added to inventories, which are part of investment, so production is counted in the year it happens.

items.q: A smartphone today costs about the same as one did ten years ago but does far more. Which limitation of GDP does this show?
options: GDP leaves out goods produced by firms based abroad
GDP counts the phone twice, once when made and once when sold
GDP leaves out goods that households buy for themselves
GDP leaves out the value of used goods sold this year
GDP counts the price paid and can miss gains in quality

why.correct: GDP adds market values. When quality rises faster than price, GDP understates how much better off people are.
options: GDP counts production inside the borders, whoever owns the firm; that is not the issue here.
A new phone is counted once, as a final good.
Household purchases are consumption, the largest part of GDP.
Used goods are left out of GDP, but that is not this example; here the price stays the same while the phone does far more.
Right: if the price is the same, GDP counts the same value, though buyers get a much better good.

items.q: One spring, 3 million students finish school in Country V and start looking for work; no one loses a job. What happens to the unemployment rate right away?
options: It rises, because new job seekers enter the labor force as unemployed
It falls, because the labor force grows
It stays the same, because no one was laid off
It rises, because the graduates were counted as employed while in school
It stays the same, because new graduates are counted once they are hired

why.correct: The unemployment rate depends on who is looking, not just on layoffs. New entrants searching for work add to frictional unemployment.
options: Right: the graduates are now available and looking, so they join the labor force as unemployed until they find jobs.
The labor force grows, but by people who are all unemployed, so the share unemployed rises.
Unemployment can rise without layoffs when new searchers enter the labor force.
Full-time students not looking for work are outside the labor force, not employed.
People without a job who are looking for one count as unemployed from the start, so the rate rises at once.

items.q: What is the value of a price index in its base year?
options: The cost of the basket in that year
The inflation rate in that year

why.correct: Every index is scaled so the base year equals 100, which makes other years easy to read as percents of it.
options: Right: the base-year cost divided by itself is 1, times 100 is 100.
The index measures cost relative to the base year; a value of 0 would mean the basket was free.
The index divides the basket's cost by its own base-year cost and multiplies by 100, so it is 100, not a dollar amount.
The ratio is 1, but an index multiplies it by 100.
The base year sets the reference point; its index is 100 whatever inflation was.

items.q: Based on the table, what was Ulma's inflation rate from Year 1 to Year 2?
options: About 4.8%

why.correct: The inflation rate is the percent change in the price index: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>126</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow><mn>120</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{126 - 120}{120} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 5\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: That compares Year 2 with the base year (100), not with Year 1.
6 is the change in index points; divide it by the old index to get a percent.

Right: divide the change in the index by the old index, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>120</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{6}{120} \times 100 = 5\%</annotation></semantics></math>.

That divides by the new index, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>6</mn><mn>126</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{6}{126}</annotation></semantics></math>; the inflation rate divides by the old one.
126 is the price index itself, not a rate of change.

items.q: Why does high, unpredictable inflation make it harder for a firm to plan a new factory?
options: Factories are not counted in GDP during inflation
The firm can't tell what future costs and prices will be
Inflation makes factories illegal to build
Inflation lowers the number of workers in the labor force
Inflation lowers the price of the machines the factory needs

why.correct: Uncertainty is a cost of inflation: when people cannot predict prices, they hesitate to sign long contracts or make long-lived investments.
options: A new factory is investment in GDP whatever the inflation rate.
Right: uncertainty about inflation makes long-term contracts and plans riskier.
No such rule exists; the problem is uncertainty about future prices.
Inflation itself does not shrink the labor force.
Inflation is a rise in the general price level; the planning problem is that future costs and prices are hard to predict.

items.q: Which is an example of a fixed income?
options: A wage that rises each year by the rise in the CPI
Profits from a business whose prices rise with inflation
Interest on a savings account whose rate is reset with inflation
A salary renegotiated each year to match prices
A pension that pays the same dollar amount every month

why.correct: A fixed income is a set number of dollars, so its purchasing power falls when prices rise.
options: That income is indexed to prices, so it is not fixed in purchasing power or in dollars.
Business income can rise as the firm raises its prices.
A rate reset with inflation keeps up with prices, so this income is not fixed in dollars.
A salary that is adjusted to prices is not fixed.
Right: its dollar amount does not change when prices rise.

items.q: In the base year, how do nominal GDP and real GDP compare?
options: They can't be compared in the base year
They are equal, and the GDP deflator is 100
Nominal GDP is larger, because it uses current prices
Real GDP is zero, because no inflation has happened yet
Real GDP is larger, because it removes inflation

why.correct: Real GDP uses base-year prices and nominal GDP uses current prices. In the base year these are the same prices, so the deflator is 100.
options: They can: they are equal by definition.
Right: in the base year, current prices are the base-year prices.
In the base year current prices are base-year prices, so the two are the same.
In the base year real GDP is output valued at base-year prices, which are that year's prices, so it equals nominal GDP.
There is nothing to remove in the base year: the prices are the same.

items.q: How can Berovia produce more than its potential output?
options: By having more workers than the adult population
By counting the same output twice in the GDP figures
By importing more goods than it exports
By moving to a point outside its PPC
By running workers and machines harder for a while

why.correct: Potential output is what the economy produces at the natural rate of unemployment. Above it, firms and workers are stretched, which can last only for a while.
options: The labor force can't exceed the adult population; output rises because people work more hours.
GDP counts final goods once; the extra output is real production.
Imports are produced abroad and do not add to Berovia's output; producing above potential comes from using resources harder for a while.
A point outside the PPC can't be reached with current resources; a boom stretches how hard they are used.
Right: potential is the sustainable full-employment level; extra shifts and overtime can push output above it temporarily.

items.q: The government cuts income taxes, and households keep more of each paycheck. What happens to aggregate demand?
options: SRAS shifts right, because workers keep more of their pay
It shifts left, because the government collects less money to spend
It shifts right, because take-home pay and consumption rise
It moves along the curve, because taxes are a kind of price
It shifts right, because the government buys more goods

why.correct: A tax cut raises households' take-home pay, so consumption and AD rise at every price level.
options: The tax cut raises disposable income and consumption, which shifts AD; SRAS depends on firms' costs of production.
A tax cut changes taxes, not the government's spending plans; G is unchanged here.
Right: lower taxes leave households more to spend, so consumption rises at every price level.
Taxes are not the price level. A tax change shifts AD through consumption.
The government did not raise its purchases here; the effect works through households' spending.

items.q: Which statement about the MPC and the MPS is correct?
options: They add up to the spending multiplier
The MPS equals 1 divided by the MPC
The MPC is consumption divided by disposable income
They add up to 1
The MPS rises whenever the MPC rises

why.correct: An extra dollar of disposable income is either consumed or saved, so MPC + MPS = 1.
