options: The multiplier is 1 / MPS, not MPC + MPS.

The MPC and MPS add up to 1, so the MPS is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mtext>MPC</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1 - \text{MPC}</annotation></semantics></math>; 1 divided by the MPS is the spending multiplier.
That is the share of all income spent. The MPC is the change in consumption over the change in disposable income.
Right: MPC + MPS = 1.
Because they add to 1, a higher MPC means a lower MPS.

items.q: In Ibera the MPC is 0.8. The government cuts taxes by $40 billion. Ignoring any effect on prices, what is the largest possible change in real GDP?
options: An increase of $160 billion
An increase of $200 billion
An increase of $40 billion
A decrease of $160 billion
An increase of $32 billion

why.correct: The tax multiplier is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>0.8</mn></mrow><mn>0.2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{-0.8}{0.2} = -4</annotation></semantics></math>. A tax change of <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-40</annotation></semantics></math> billion changes real GDP by <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>×</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>160</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-40 \times -4 = 160</annotation></semantics></math> billion dollars, an increase.
options: Right: a tax cut of 40 billion times a tax multiplier of size 4 raises real GDP by 160 billion.
That uses the spending multiplier, 5; part of a tax cut is saved first, so the tax multiplier is one smaller.
The tax cut sets off rounds of spending, so output changes by more than the cut itself.
A tax cut raises disposable income and consumption, so real GDP rises; the minus sign of the tax multiplier is for a tax increase.

$32 billion is the first round of spending, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.8</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.8 \times 40</annotation></semantics></math>; later rounds add more.

items.q: A country's government adds many new safety rules that raise firms' costs of producing each unit. What happens to SRAS?
options: LRAS shifts right
It shifts right
It shifts left
It does not change, because rules are not prices
It becomes vertical

why.correct: Government rules and taxes that raise firms' costs shift SRAS left; subsidies shift it right.
options: Rules that raise the cost of each unit lower what firms supply at each price level; they shift SRAS left and add no capacity.
Higher costs mean less supply at each price level, not more.
Right: rules that raise costs per unit lower the output firms supply at each price level.
Rules that raise costs work like a higher input price: they shift SRAS.
The slope comes from sticky wages and prices in the short run; a cost increase shifts the curve.

items.q: From 2020 to 2030, how would Country L's production possibilities curve (PPC) change, and why?
options: It would shift inward, because more of the resources are used
It would shift inward, because the population grew
It would not change, because a PPC shows just two goods
It would shift outward, as labor and capital grew
The economy would move from a point inside the PPC to a point on it

why.correct: A rise in resources moves full-employment output and the PPC together: LRAS right, PPC out.
options: Using more resources does not shrink what can be made; more resources move the PPC out.
More labor and capital raise what the economy can produce, so the curve shifts outward, not inward.
The PPC shows the limits on producing two goods, and those limits widen with more resources.
Right: LRAS shifting right and the PPC shifting out show the same rise in productive capacity.
That is a fall in unemployment of existing resources. Here the resources themselves grew.

items.q: On an AD-AS graph, the short-run equilibrium is at PL1 and Y1, and Y1 is to the right of LRAS. Where should YF be labeled?
options: On the horizontal axis where LRAS stands, to the left of Y1
On the horizontal axis at Y1, where AD crosses SRAS
On the vertical axis at PL1, level with the equilibrium
On the horizontal axis to the right of Y1, beyond the equilibrium
On the vertical axis where AD meets LRAS

why.correct: Label YF where LRAS meets the real GDP axis; with Y1 to its right, the gap between them is the inflationary gap.
options: Right: YF is full-employment output, where the vertical LRAS meets the real GDP axis.
Y1 is actual output. In an inflationary gap it is to the right of YF.
YF is an output level, so it goes on the real GDP axis.
Y1 is right of LRAS, so YF lies to the left of Y1.
YF is a level of real GDP, so it goes on the horizontal axis where LRAS stands, not on the price level axis.

items.q: Based on the table, which shift best explains the change from Year 3 to Year 4?
options: SRAS shifted left: the price level fell and real GDP fell
SRAS shifted right: the price level fell and real GDP fell
AD shifted left: the price level and real GDP both fell
AD shifted right: unemployment rose
AD shifted right: the price level and real GDP both rose

why.correct: From Year 3 to Year 4 the price level fell (110 to 108), real GDP fell and unemployment rose: AD shifted left.
options: A leftward SRAS shift raises the price level; here it fell.
A rightward SRAS shift raises real GDP; here it fell.
Right: both falling together, with unemployment rising, is a negative demand shock.
More AD raises output and lowers unemployment.
From Year 3 to Year 4 the price level fell from 110 to 108 and real GDP from 820 to 790, so AD shifted left.

items.q: In Merovia, what is the short-run effect of the two shocks on the price level?
options: It falls
It stays the same, because the shocks cancel
It rises
It falls at first, then returns to its old level
It depends on the sizes of the two shocks

why.correct: SRAS shifts left and AD shifts right: each alone raises the price level, so together it surely rises.
options: Neither shock lowers the price level; both raise it.
They cancel for output, perhaps, but both push the price level the same way: up.
Right: the fuel shock (SRAS left) and the export boom (AD right) both push the price level up.
Higher fuel costs shift SRAS left and the foreign boom shifts AD right; both push the price level up at once.
The sizes matter for output, not for the price level, which both shocks raise.

items.q: A student writes: "In a recessionary gap, the economy returns to full employment because aggregate demand recovers." What is wrong with this as an explanation of long-run self-adjustment?
options: Self-adjustment works through rising nominal wages shifting SRAS left
Nothing is wrong: AD shifts right as people regain confidence
It names AD; the mechanism is LRAS shifting right
It names AD; the mechanism is falling wages shifting SRAS right
Self-adjustment works through LRAS shifting left to meet AD

why.correct: The mechanism readers look for: unemployment above the natural rate lowers nominal wages and input prices, so SRAS shifts right.
options: Rising wages describe an inflationary gap. In a recessionary gap wages fall.
If spending recovers that is a new demand shock, not self-adjustment, which runs through wages and SRAS.
LRAS stays where it is; the economy returns to it because falling nominal wages shift SRAS right.
Right: with no policy, spending is unchanged; lower wages and input prices shift SRAS.
LRAS depends on resources and technology, which did not change.

items.q: A drought shifts SRAS left and the economy falls into a recessionary gap. If the drought ends and no policy is used, how does the economy return to full employment?
options: Lower wages and input prices shift SRAS back right
Rising prices raise profits, so firms hire more until output is back
AD shifts left to meet LRAS
LRAS shifts left to meet the new equilibrium
The government raises spending to shift AD right

why.correct: With output below full employment, wages and input prices fall and SRAS shifts right until output is back at YF.
options: Right: the same SRAS mechanism closes a gap however it began.
In a recessionary gap the price level falls as SRAS shifts right.
A leftward AD shift would lower output further.
LRAS moves only with resources and technology. A temporary drought does not lower capacity for good.
The question says no policy is used; lower wages and input prices shift SRAS back right on their own.

items.q: The government raises spending to close a recessionary gap. Compared with waiting for the economy to adjust on its own, what is different about the price level when output reaches full employment?
options: It is lower, because the government buys goods at lower prices
It is higher, because AD shifted right instead of SRAS
It is lower, because the gap closes sooner
It is the same, because both end at full employment
It is lower, because spending shifts SRAS right

why.correct: Closing a recessionary gap with AD (fiscal policy) ends at a higher price level; closing it through falling wages (SRAS right) ends at a lower one.
options: Government purchases add to spending, which raises the price level.
Right: fiscal policy moves the economy up along SRAS; self-adjustment moves it down along AD.
Closing the gap sooner does not lower prices; spending shifts AD right, so the price level ends higher than with self-adjustment.
Both reach YF, but by different curves, so the price levels differ.
Government spending is part of AD; it does not lower firms' costs.

items.q: The graph shows Toren's economy. Which fiscal policy would move real GDP toward full employment?
options: A rise in government purchases
A cut in income taxes
A rise in transfer payments
A cut in government purchases
A cut in the interest rate on reserve balances

why.correct: Output is above full employment (right of LRAS): an inflationary gap. Contractionary fiscal policy, such as less government purchasing, shifts AD left toward LRAS.
options: More purchases shift AD right, away from full employment, since output is already above it.
A tax cut raises consumption and shifts AD right, widening the inflationary gap.
Higher transfers raise disposable income and consumption, so AD shifts right and the gap widens.
Right: lower government purchases shift AD left, lowering output toward full employment and easing the price level.
That is a monetary policy action, and lowering the administered rate would push AD right, the wrong way here.

items.q: Why can automatic stabilizers act faster than discretionary fiscal policy?
options: They have a larger multiplier than government purchases
They act on SRAS, which moves faster than AD
They need no new decision to take effect
The central bank decides when they start
They are set by firms, which react faster than governments

why.correct: Discretionary policy has to be recognized, decided and carried out; automatic stabilizers respond as soon as incomes change.
options: Their speed comes from needing no decision, not from a bigger multiplier.
They act on disposable income and spending, which is AD.
Right: the rules are already in place, so payments and taxes respond at once.
Automatic stabilizers are parts of the tax and transfer system; they act without a new decision by the central bank or the legislature.
They are government tax and transfer rules, not decisions by firms.

items.q: Why is an interest rate called the price of borrowing?
options: It is the fee a bank charges to open an account
It is the yearly cost of using borrowed money, as a percent
It is the total amount a borrower repays at the end of the loan
It is the price of the goods bought with the loan
It is the share of a deposit a bank keeps as reserves

why.correct: The interest rate is the yearly cost of borrowing, as a percent of the amount borrowed; to a lender it is the reward for lending.
options: An account fee is not interest. Interest is paid for the use of borrowed money over time.
Right: a 6% rate means $6 a year for each $100 borrowed.
The total repaid includes the amount borrowed; the rate is the yearly charge as a percent.
The goods have their own prices. Interest is the cost of the borrowed money itself.
That describes a reserve ratio; an interest rate is the yearly cost of borrowing, as a percent of the loan.

items.q: What does Loan D's real interest rate tell its lender?
options: The lender expects to lose money in dollars
The lender expects inflation of zero
The lender expects no gain in buying power
The lender expects to earn 5% more buying power
The loan pays no interest in dollars

why.correct: A zero real rate means the interest just offsets the expected inflation rate: dollars grow, buying power does not.
options: In dollars the lender gains 5%; it is buying power that stays the same.

Loan D's lender expects inflation of 5%; the real rate is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\% - 5\% = 0</annotation></semantics></math>, which means no gain in buying power.
Right: 5% - 5% = 0%, so the extra dollars just keep up with the expected inflation rate.
That would need a 5% real rate. Here the expected inflation rate cancels the 5% nominal rate.
It pays 5% in dollars. Zero is the real rate, not the nominal one.

items.q: A bank in Merrin lends for one year at a fixed nominal rate of 7%, expecting inflation of 2%. Inflation turns out to be 4%. What real interest rate does the bank earn?

why.correct: The real rate earned is the nominal rate minus the inflation that actually happened: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>%</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7\% - 4\% = 3\%</annotation></semantics></math>. The bank expected <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>%</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7\% - 2\% = 5\%</annotation></semantics></math>, so the surprise inflation cost it buying power.
options: That adds expected inflation to the nominal rate; the real rate is the nominal rate minus inflation.
5% is the real rate the bank expected when it made the loan; inflation came in higher.
That adds inflation to the nominal rate; the real rate subtracts it.
2% is the surprise in inflation (4% minus 2%), not the real rate the bank earns.

Right: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo>%</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>%</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7\% - 4\% = 3\%</annotation></semantics></math>, using the inflation that actually happened.

items.q: Lee deposits $200 of cash into his checking account. What happens to M1 right away?
options: It rises by $200
It falls by $200
It rises by $2,000 as the bank lends
It stays the same
It rises by $400

why.correct: Moving money between two parts of M1 leaves M1 unchanged. (What the bank then lends is the next topic.)
options: The new deposit adds $200, but $200 of currency left the public's hands, so M1 does not change.
The currency is gone, but the checkable deposit replaces it, so M1 is unchanged.
Right away, $200 of cash in M1 becomes $200 of checkable deposits in M1, so M1 is unchanged; any lending comes later.
Right: currency (in M1) becomes a checkable deposit (also in M1).
Nothing is counted twice: one part of M1 swaps for another.

items.q: With limited reserves, banks lend all of their excess reserves. The central bank raises the required reserve ratio from 0.1 to 0.2. What happens to the money multiplier?
options: It doubles from 10 to 20
It falls from 10 to 5
It falls from 20 to 10
It rises from 5 to 10
It stays at 10, since deposits are unchanged

why.correct: The money multiplier is 1 / required reserve ratio, so a higher ratio means a smaller multiplier and less money creation.
options: A higher ratio means banks lend less of each deposit, so the multiplier falls.

With a ratio of 0.1 the money multiplier is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>0.1</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{0.1} = 10</annotation></semantics></math>, and with 0.2 it is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>0.2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{0.2} = 5</annotation></semantics></math>.
At 0.1 the multiplier is 10, and at 0.2 it is 5; it falls.
The multiplier depends on the ratio, so it changes when the ratio does.

items.q: Why is the money supply drawn as a vertical line on the money market graph?
options: People want the same amount of money at any interest rate
Banks hold more reserves when interest rates rise
The central bank sets the quantity of money, whatever the interest rate
Money demand is vertical, so money supply is drawn the same way
The quantity of money grows as interest rates rise

why.correct: In the money market model the central bank fixes the quantity of money, so the money supply curve is vertical.
options: That would describe money demand, which slopes down.
The graph treats the quantity of money as set by the central bank, not by rates.
Right: the quantity does not respond to the rate, so supply is vertical.
Money demand slopes down; the money supply is vertical because the central bank sets its quantity.
That would be an upward-sloping supply curve, not a vertical one.

items.q: What goes on the vertical axis of the money market graph?
options: The real interest rate
The price level
The nominal interest rate
The inflation rate
The quantity of money

why.correct: Money market: nominal interest rate (vertical) and quantity of money (horizontal). Writing "real" loses the graph point.
options: The real rate goes on a different graph later in this unit. The money market uses the nominal rate.
The price level goes on the AD-AS graph.
Right: the opportunity cost of holding money is the nominal rate.
The vertical axis is the nominal interest rate, the opportunity cost of holding money instead of bonds.
The quantity of money is on the horizontal axis.

items.q: With ample reserves, what is the central bank's main tool for moving the policy rate?
options: Printing currency to pay for government spending
Changing the required reserve ratio
Buying and selling bonds to shift reserve supply
Setting its administered rates, mainly interest on reserve balances
Changing taxes and government spending

why.correct: With ample reserves, administered rates (interest on reserve balances and the overnight reverse repurchase rate) set the policy rate.
options: With ample reserves the central bank moves the policy rate with its administered rates; paying for government spending is not a monetary policy tool.
With ample reserves, banks hold far more than required, so the ratio does not bind.
In the ample range, shifting reserve supply does not move the rate.
Right: the policy rate follows the rates the central bank pays.
That is fiscal policy, set by the government, not the central bank.

items.q: Which economic problem is the policy in the graph most likely aimed at, and what is its short-run effect on aggregate demand?
options: An inflationary gap; aggregate demand falls
A recessionary gap; aggregate demand falls
An inflationary gap; aggregate demand rises
A recessionary gap; aggregate demand rises
Neither gap; aggregate demand does not change

why.correct: Lowering the policy rate is expansionary monetary policy, used to close a recessionary gap by raising aggregate demand.
options: A lower policy rate is expansionary: it raises aggregate demand, which would widen an inflationary gap.
Lower interest rates raise spending, so aggregate demand rises, not falls.
Raising AD in an inflationary gap would push prices higher; this policy fits a recession.
Right: lower rates raise investment and consumption, so AD shifts right and output rises.
The graph shows a change in the policy rate, and a change in interest rates shifts AD in the short run.

items.q: Glenna's central bank works with limited reserves. Which open market operation could cause the change shown in the graph, and what happens to the prices of bonds already issued?
options: Buying government bonds; bond prices rise
Selling government bonds; bond prices fall
Selling government bonds; bond prices rise
Buying government bonds; bond prices fall
Lowering the discount rate; bond prices fall

why.correct: The money supply shifted left and the nominal interest rate rose. Selling bonds takes reserves out of banks, so the money supply falls. Bond prices and interest rates move in opposite directions, so existing bonds fall in price.
options: Buying bonds adds reserves and raises the money supply, which shifts MS right; the graph shows it shifting left.
Right: a bond sale lowers reserves and the money supply, the interest rate rises and bond prices fall.
A higher interest rate makes existing bonds with lower rates less attractive, so their prices fall, not rise.
Buying bonds would raise the money supply and lower the interest rate, the opposite of the graph.
A lower discount rate encourages banks to borrow reserves, which raises the money supply rather than lowering it.

items.q: Brin raises taxes so that tax revenue equals government spending, and private saving stays at 400. What happens to national saving and the real interest rate?
options: National saving falls and the real rate rises
National saving rises to 400 and the real rate falls
Both are unchanged, since private saving is the same
National saving rises and the real rate rises
National saving falls to 300 and the real rate falls

why.correct: Less government borrowing means more national saving and a lower real interest rate.
options: Public saving rises from -100 to 0, so national saving rises, not falls.
Right: with no government borrowing, there is less demand for loanable funds, so the real rate falls.
Public saving changed from -100 to 0, so national saving changes.
Less government borrowing lowers the real interest rate.

National saving starts at <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>400</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>300</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">400 - 100 = 300</annotation></semantics></math>, with the deficit of 100 subtracted; balancing the budget raises it to 400, so it rises, and the real rate falls.

items.q: In the graph, what happens to the quantity of loanable funds?
options: It rises, because the supply of loanable funds shifted right
It falls, because the real interest rate rose
It stays the same, because saving did not change
It is not shown on the graph
It rises, as savers lend more at the higher rate

why.correct: When demand shifts right along an upward-sloping supply curve, both the real interest rate and the quantity rise.
options: The supply curve did not move; demand shifted right, the real rate rose, and savers lent more along the supply curve.
A higher rate cuts borrowing along the old demand, but here demand shifted right.
Saving rises along the supply curve as the real rate rises.
One curve shifted, so both changes are clear: the rate and the quantity rise.
Right: the higher real rate draws out more saving, a movement along supply.

items.q: Sundra's central bank lowers its administered rates and, at the same time, the legislature raises government spending. Compared with either policy alone, what happens to AD and to the interest rates banks charge on loans?
options: AD rises by more; loan rates fall for sure
AD rises by more; loan rates rise for sure
AD rises by more; the effect on loan rates is indeterminate
The effect on AD is indeterminate, and loan rates fall for sure
AD is unchanged; the interest rate falls for sure

why.correct: When two policies push AD the same way, the AD effect is clear and the effect on loan rates is the one that depends on sizes. (The policy rate itself falls, because it follows the administered rates; loan rates also feel the extra borrowing and spending.)
options: The monetary move pulls loan rates down, but the higher spending and income raise the demand for money and for borrowing, which push them up.
The fiscal move pushes loan rates up, but the lower administered rate pulls them down. Without the sizes you cannot say which wins.
Right: both policies push AD right. The spending rise pushes loan rates up while the monetary move pulls them down, so the net change cannot be told without sizes.
Both policies are expansionary, so they push AD the same way. It is loan rates whose change is unclear.
Both policies are expansionary, so AD rises by more than with either one alone.

items.q: Kalvo's legislature raises government spending while its central bank, which operates with ample reserves, raises the interest rate on reserve balances. What happens to interest rates and to aggregate demand in the short run?
options: Interest rates rise; aggregate demand rises
Interest rates rise; the effect on aggregate demand is indeterminate
The effect on interest rates is indeterminate; aggregate demand falls
Interest rates fall; aggregate demand rises
Interest rates rise; aggregate demand falls

why.correct: Both actions push interest rates up: more government spending raises borrowing and money demand, and a higher administered rate raises the policy rate. But they push AD in opposite directions (spending raises it, higher rates lower investment), so without their sizes the change in AD is indeterminate.
options: The higher administered rate lowers investment and consumption, which pulls AD down; without the sizes, AD may rise or fall.
Right: both actions raise interest rates, while their pulls on AD go opposite ways.
Both actions push interest rates the same way, up, so that change is determinate; it is AD that cannot be signed.
A higher interest rate on reserve balances raises the policy rate, so interest rates do not fall.
Higher government spending pushes AD up while the higher rate pulls it down, so a fall is not certain.

items.q: Which feature of the AD-AS model matches the long-run Phillips curve?
options: SRAS, which slopes up
LRAS, vertical at full-employment output
The PPC, which bows outward
AD, which slopes down
The point where AD crosses SRAS in the short run

why.correct: LRAS and LRPC both mark full employment: real GDP at potential, unemployment at the natural rate.
options: SRAS shifts match SRPC shifts in the opposite direction; it is not the long-run curve.
Right: full-employment output on LRAS is the output at which unemployment equals the natural rate, where LRPC stands.
The PPC is not part of the AD-AS model; the LRPC matches LRAS, both vertical at full employment.
AD shifts are movements along the SRPC.
That is the short-run equilibrium, which can sit off LRPC.

items.q: Yarrow's natural rate of unemployment is 5%, and inflation has been steady at 2%. Its central bank raises aggregate demand again and again to hold unemployment at 3%. What happens over time?
options: The LRPC shifts left to 3%, and inflation returns to 2%
Inflation settles at a higher, steady rate, with unemployment held at 3% for good
Inflation keeps rising, as expected inflation catches up and the SRPC shifts up each time
Unemployment stays at 3%, and inflation falls back to 2% as prices adjust
The SRPC shifts down each time, so inflation falls

why.correct: Holding unemployment below the natural rate works only while inflation is higher than expected. As people come to expect the higher inflation, the SRPC shifts up, so the central bank needs ever higher inflation to keep unemployment at 3%. In the long run there is no trade-off: the LRPC stays at 5%.
options: The natural rate depends on frictional and structural unemployment, not on demand, so the LRPC stays at 5%.
A steady higher inflation rate would come to be expected, and then unemployment would return to 5%; holding 3% needs rising inflation.
Right: each time expectations catch up, the SRPC shifts up, so holding unemployment at 3% takes ever higher inflation.
With demand pushed up again and again, inflation rises rather than falling back.
Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC up, not down.

items.q: What does the velocity of money measure?
options: How many times a year the average dollar is spent on final goods and services
How fast the central bank adds new money to the economy
The share of extra income that people save
How quickly prices rise over a year
How many times a new deposit is lent and re-lent through the whole banking system

why.correct: From <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M \times V = P \times Y</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mi>M</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V = \frac{P \times Y}{M}</annotation></semantics></math>, nominal GDP per dollar of money.
options: Right: velocity is nominal GDP divided by the money supply.
That is the money growth rate, M changing, not V.
That is the MPS; velocity is how many times a year the average dollar is spent on final output.
That is the inflation rate.
That describes the money multiplier process, not velocity.

items.q: In Evrin, the money supply is $500 billion, the price level is 2 and real GDP is $1,000 billion. What is the velocity of money?

why.correct: From <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M \times V = P \times Y</annotation></semantics></math>, velocity is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><mi>M</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{P \times Y}{M}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mn>500</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{2 \times 1{,}000}{500}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 4</annotation></semantics></math>: the average dollar is spent on final output 4 times a year.
options: That adds nominal GDP and the money supply; velocity is their ratio.

That divides the money supply by nominal GDP, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>500</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{500}{2{,}000}</annotation></semantics></math>; velocity is nominal GDP divided by money.

That divides real GDP by money and leaves out the price level; velocity uses nominal GDP, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P \times Y</annotation></semantics></math>.

Right: nominal GDP is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2 \times 1{,}000 = 2{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> billion, and <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>000</mn></mrow><mn>500</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2{,}000}{500} = 4</annotation></semantics></math>.
That subtracts the money supply from nominal GDP; velocity divides nominal GDP by money.

items.q: During a recession, a legislature cuts taxes and raises spending to close the gap. What happens to the budget?
options: The deficit shrinks, because the policy raises output
The national debt falls, because the economy recovers
A surplus appears, because output rises
The deficit grows (or a surplus shrinks)
Nothing changes, because the two policies cancel out

why.correct: Expansionary fiscal policy raises the deficit; contractionary fiscal policy lowers it.
options: Higher output brings in some tax revenue, but the tax cuts and new spending widen the deficit.
The added borrowing adds to the debt.
Lower taxes and more spending widen the deficit; a recovery may offset part of it, not turn it into a surplus.
Right: lower revenue and higher outlays widen the gap between them.
Both a tax cut and a spending rise widen the deficit; they do not cancel.

items.q: What is crowding out?
options: A fall in government spending when a boom in private investment raises interest rates
A fall in private investment when government borrowing raises the real interest rate
A rise in imports when government spending raises incomes
A rise in prices when too much money chases too few goods
A rise in private investment when government spending raises demand

why.correct: Crowding out: deficit spending financed by borrowing raises the real interest rate and lowers private investment.
options: Crowding out runs the other way: government borrowing displaces private investment.
Right: the government's demand for funds pushes up the real rate, and interest-sensitive private spending falls.
Higher income does raise imports, but that is not crowding out.
That describes inflation from money growth.
That is the opposite effect; crowding out is a fall in private investment as government borrowing raises the real rate.

items.q: Which change in Garrow would reduce the crowding out of private investment caused by the government's borrowing?
options: A rise in government borrowing that shifts the demand for loanable funds right
A fall in private saving that shifts the supply of loanable funds left
A fall in the real interest rate caused by more government borrowing
A rise in expected inflation that raises nominal interest rates
A rise in private saving that shifts the supply of loanable funds right

why.correct: Crowding out depends on how far the real interest rate rises; more saving limits the rise.
options: More government borrowing would raise the rate further and crowd out more investment.
Less saving raises the real rate, adding to crowding out.
More government borrowing raises the real interest rate, which is what crowds out investment; it does not lower it.
A higher nominal rate driven by expected inflation does not lower the real rate firms face.
Right: more saving pushes the real rate back down, so less private investment is crowded out.

items.q: A nurse completes a two-year course that lets her do more complex work. In growth terms, what has increased?
options: Human capital
Financial capital
Physical capital
Natural resources
Aggregate demand

why.correct: Human capital: education, training, experience and health that raise what a worker can produce.
options: Right: the skills and knowledge workers gain through education and training are human capital.
Financial capital is money raised to invest; the nurse's new skill is human capital, the knowledge and skill of workers.
Physical capital is equipment, buildings and machines, not skills.
Natural resources are land, minerals, water and the like.
Training changes what a worker can produce, not total spending.

items.q: Alton and Breck both raised real GDP by 10 percent. Why did only Alton's real GDP per capita rise?
options: Breck's price level rose faster, so its real GDP did not really grow
Alton's nominal GDP rose faster than Breck's
Alton's population fell, so each person got more of the same output
Breck's figures are nominal GDP, which overstates growth
Breck's population grew as fast as its output did

why.correct: To raise living standards, output must grow faster than population.
options: The table is in base-year dollars, so price changes are already removed.
Both raised real GDP by 10 percent; per capita growth depends on population, and Breck's grew as fast as its output.
Alton's population stayed at 20 million; its output rose.
Both countries' figures are real GDP.
Right: per capita growth is roughly output growth minus population growth: 10 - 10 = 0 for Breck.

items.q: Stronger patent protection for new inventions is a policy aimed mainly at which source of growth?
options: Human capital
Physical capital
Technology
Natural resources
Aggregate demand

why.correct: Research funding and patents target technology.
options: Human capital is workers' skills and education.
Patents reward invention, which is new technology; physical capital is machines, tools and buildings.
Right: patents let inventors earn a return on new ideas, which encourages research and new methods.
Patents cover ideas, not land or minerals.
Patents work on the supply side, through innovation.

items.q: What is supply-side fiscal policy?
options: Central bank actions that change the supply of money
Changes in government spending meant to raise AD in a recession, with no aim at capacity
Tax and spending changes meant to raise incentives to work, save and invest, shifting LRAS right
Limits on how much firms may produce
Lowering interest rates to raise investment

why.correct: Supply-side policies target LRAS through incentives and investment.
options: That is monetary policy.
That is demand-side (stabilization) fiscal policy.
Right: supply-side policy aims at the economy's capacity, not just at spending.
Supply-side policy aims to raise production, not limit it.
That is monetary policy; supply-side fiscal policy uses taxes and spending to raise incentives and shift LRAS right.

items.q: Over ten years Pirel's production possibilities curve changes as the graph shows. Which policy most likely contributed?
options: Tax credits that raise private investment in new equipment
A cut in the interest rate on reserve balances during a recession
A one-time rise in transfer payments
Limits on the number of hours people may work
Higher taxes on income from saving and investment

why.correct: The PPC shifted outward: the economy can produce more of both goods. A tax credit for investment adds to the capital stock, which raises productive capacity over time (and shifts LRAS right).
options: Right: more physical capital raises what the economy can produce, so the PPC shifts out over the years.
A lower policy rate in a recession raises AD and moves the economy toward its PPC; it is not mainly a capacity policy.
Transfers raise spending (AD) for a while; they do not add to resources or technology.
Fewer hours of labor would shift the PPC inward, not outward.
Taxing saving and investment more lowers the incentive to build capital, which slows growth.

items.q: Firms in Arland pay interest to foreign holders of their bonds. How is the interest payment recorded in Arland's balance of payments?
options: As a debit in the current account (income paid abroad)
As a credit in the capital and financial account
As a debit in the capital and financial account
As a credit in the current account (income received)
It is not recorded, because no good changes hands

why.correct: Income paid to foreigners (interest, dividends) is a current account debit.
options: Right: interest and dividends paid to foreigners are income payments, recorded in the current account as a debit.
Interest paid abroad is income leaving the country, a debit in the current account; it is not a sale of a financial asset.
The bonds were an asset trade when they were sold, but interest on them is income, which goes in the current account.
The money leaves Arland, so it is a debit, not a credit.
Income flows are part of the current account even though no good or service is traded.

items.q: An Arland student pays tuition in Belvia that is fixed in bels. Which change makes the semester cheaper for the student, in arls?
options: The rate moves from 4 bels per arl to 3 bels per arl
The rate moves from 4 bels per arl to 2 bels per arl
The rate moves from 3 bels per arl to 4 bels per arl
The rate moves from 0.25 arl per bel to 0.30 arl per bel
The tuition rises in bels while the rate stays the same

why.correct: The student gains when the arl appreciates: more bels per arl.
options: Each arl buys fewer bels, so the same bel tuition costs more arls.
Fewer bels per arl means each bel costs more arls, so the tuition fixed in bels costs the student more.
Right: each arl now buys more bels, so the bel tuition takes fewer arls. The arl appreciated.
Each bel now costs more arls, so the tuition costs more arls. The bel appreciated.
A higher bel price at the same rate costs more arls.

items.q: Why does the demand curve for arls slope down?
options: When the arl is cheaper in bels, Arland goods cost Belvians fewer bels, so they want more arls
When the arl is cheaper, Arland residents want to sell more arls
When the arl is cheaper, Arland interest rates rise
When the arl is cheaper, Belvian goods cost Arland residents fewer arls
When the arl is cheaper, Belvians earn more bels

why.correct: A lower price of the arl makes Arland goods and assets cheaper for Belvians, so they want more arls.
options: Right: a lower price of the arl makes everything priced in arls cheaper for Belvians, so the quantity of arls demanded rises.
That describes the supply side, and in fact a cheaper arl makes Arland residents offer fewer arls.
The price of the arl does not set interest rates; interest rates are a separate shifter.
A cheaper arl makes Belvian goods cost Arland residents more arls, not fewer.
Belvian incomes in bels do not change with the price of the arl; Arland goods cost fewer bels, so Belvians want more arls.

items.q: Currency traders come to expect that the bel will appreciate against the arl next month. What happens in the market for bels now?
options: Demand for bels falls, since traders wait for next month
Supply of bels falls next month, so nothing changes now
Supply of bels rises, so the bel depreciates now
Nothing happens until the appreciation arrives
Demand for bels rises now, so the bel appreciates now

why.correct: Expected appreciation raises demand for a currency today.
options: Traders who expect a rise want to buy before it happens, which raises demand now.
Expectations act now: traders buy bels today to gain from the expected rise, so demand for bels rises and the bel appreciates now.
Holders of bels who expect a rise are less willing to sell them, not more.
Expectations act at once: buying in advance moves the price today.
Right: traders buy bels today to sell them later at a higher price, so demand rises and the bel appreciates now.

items.q: Arland trades with Belvia alone. What happened to Belvia's net exports?
options: They fell, along with Arland's
They did not change, since the arl changed value
They fell, because Belvian goods became dearer
They rose by twice the amount Arland's fell
They rose by the amount Arland's fell

why.correct: One country's net exports are the other's net imports.
options: Arland's imports are Belvia's exports, so when Arland's net exports fall, Belvia's rise.
The bel depreciated against the arl in the same move, which makes Belvian goods cheaper in Arland.
The bel depreciated, so Belvian goods became cheaper for Arland buyers.
With two countries trading with each other alone, one's net exports are the other's net imports, so Belvia's rose by exactly what Arland's fell.
Right: with two countries, Arland's exports are Belvia's imports and Arland's imports are Belvia's exports, so Belvia's net exports rose by 70 billion arls' worth.

items.q: Compared with an economy closed to foreign savers, how does the inflow of foreign saving change the effect of more government borrowing on Arland's real interest rate?
options: The real rate rises by more, because foreigners also borrow
The real rate rises by less, because foreign saving adds to the supply of loanable funds
The real rate falls, because the inflow is larger than the new borrowing
The real rate is unaffected, because foreign saving goes to the currency market
The real rate rises by more, because the arl appreciates

why.correct: Capital inflows add to the supply of loanable funds, so the real rate rises less than it would in a closed economy.
options: Foreign savers are lenders here; they add to the supply of loanable funds.
Right: the inflow shifts the supply of loanable funds right, which holds down the rise in the real interest rate and so softens the crowding out of private investment.
The inflow happens only while Arland's real rate stays above Belvia's, so it limits the rise rather than reversing it.
The funds pass through the currency market, but they are then lent in Arland's loanable funds market.
The appreciation follows the inflow; the inflow itself adds to the supply of loanable funds, so the real rate rises by less.

items.q: Based on the table, which way does financial capital tend to flow between Dovar and Lisk, and what happens to the value of the dov?
options: Neither way, because both real rates are positive
Into Lisk; the dov depreciates
Into Lisk; the dov appreciates
Into Dovar; the dov depreciates
Into Dovar; the dov appreciates

Lisk's nominal rate is higher, but its real rate (2%) is lower; capital follows the real rate.
Capital flows to the higher real rate, which is Dovar's, and buying Dovar's assets raises the demand for dovs.
Investors buying Dovar's assets need dovs, so the demand for dovs rises and it appreciates.
Right: Dovar's real rate of 4% beats Lisk's 2%, so capital flows into Dovar and the demand for dovs rises.
